papers.title: Smartwatch-based pelvic tracking system for augmented reality navigation in total hip arthroplasty: a preliminary clinical study
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Accurate assessment of pelvic orientation is essential for acetabular cup placement during total hip arthroplasty (THA). Conventional pelvic tracking systems generally rely on dedicated tracking hardware and optical tracking infrastructure. We developed a smartwatch-based pelvic tracking system integrated with an augmented reality (AR) navigation platform and evaluated its preliminary clinical performance. Methods This retrospective study included 30 hips of 27 consecutive patients who underwent primary THA using a smartwatch-based pelvic tracking navigation system between May 2025 and April 2026. The system utilizes a commercially available smartwatch fixed to the iliac crest as a pelvic tracking device and communicates orientation information to a smartphone-based AR navigation platform via Bluetooth. Acetabular cup orientation was evaluated using postoperative CT. Absolute radiographic inclination (RI) and anteversion (RA) errors were calculated as absolute differences between the final intraoperative navigation measurements and postoperative CT measurements. Results The mean absolute RI error was 2.8° ± 2.1°, and the mean absolute RA error was 3.6° ± 2.2°. Postoperative CT measurements were within 5° of the final intraoperative navigation measurements for RI and RA in 86.7% and 70.0% of hips, respectively. Navigation was successfully completed in all 30 hips, with no conversion to a backup technique. Additional bench testing demonstrated reproducible smartwatch reattachment and reduction of time-dependent relative orientation differences following FPP invocation. Conclusions This study demonstrated the feasibility of integrating a commercially available smartwatch into a pelvic tracking system for THA navigation. The smartwatch-based pelvic tracking platform achieved a preliminary range of cup-positioning accuracy without requiring continuous optical visualization of a pelvic reference marker while utilizing a compact and widely available consumer wearable device. This study represents the first step toward wearable-device-based navigation in arthroplasty.

papers.title: Microcomputed Tomography-derived Finite Element Evaluation of Osseointegration Dynamics and Bone-Implant Bond Strength.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The integration of microcomputed tomography (microCT) with finite element modeling (FEM) offers a powerful nondestructive approach for evaluating bone-implant interactions. This research was done to investigate osseointegration dynamics and bone-implant bond strength using microCT-derived finite element analysis (FEA). MATERIALS AND METHODS: A total of 264 subjects were divided equally into control and experimental groups. High-resolution microCT imaging was performed to quantify peri-implant bone morphology, followed by specimen-specific FEM using validated computational platforms. Morphometric parameters including bone volume fraction, trabecular thickness, and bone-implant contact (BIC) were analyzed alongside biomechanical indices such as von Mises stress, strain distribution, and interfacial micromotion. Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS and GraphPad Prism, with significance set at P < 0.05. RESULTS: The experimental group demonstrated significantly improved peri-implant bone architecture, with higher bone volume fraction and increased BIC compared to controls (P < 0.001). FEA revealed reduced stress concentration, lower interfacial micromotion, and improved load distribution in the experimental group. Strong positive correlations were observed between microCT-derived parameters and implant bond strength, particularly BIC (r = 0.88, P < 0.001), indicating a direct structure-function relationship in osseointegration. CONCLUSION: The integration of microCT imaging with FEM provides a robust, nondestructive, and highly sensitive framework for evaluating osseointegration dynamics. Microstructural bone parameters are strongly predictive of biomechanical implant stability.

papers.title: Robotic winding of wet-spun fibers for biofabrication of aligned, perfusable, muscle-based tissue.
papers.abstract: Structural alignment of muscle and integrated vasculature enables the function of geometrically complex tissues in the body, such as the gastroesophageal junction and the ventricles. However, replicating this complexity is an ongoing challenge. Described here is the wet-spun & robotically articulated placement (WRAP) method for deposition of aligned cellular fibers on scaffolds, resulting in large structures fabricated from the inside-out. WRAP enables complex, multi-oriented muscle and vascular placement by creating a continuous cellular fiber through wet spinning, and then using a robotic arm programmed with a set of tissue profiles to maneuver the fiber around an organ scaffold. Wet-spun fibers, consisting of muscle cells combined with endothelial cell fibers via double-core spinning, exhibited the ability to mature, align, contract, and initiate tubulogenesis, creating perfusable fibers. Further, the robotic arm could accurately create physiologically relevant fiber patterns with high precision. The potential to generate perfusable blood vessels alongside functional muscle is paramount to fabricating muscle-based constructs. The WRAP method offers a high throughput and versatile solution to the scale-up problem plaguing the biofabrication of muscle-based tissues.

papers.title: DynaSolver: A Neural Operator for Autoregressive 4D Flow Prediction with Dynamic Boundaries
papers.abstract: Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD), but most are designed for static geometries and are not equipped to model unsteady flows induced by continuously moving boundaries. We study dynamic-boundary 4D CFD prediction for articulated moving geometries and introduce RoboCFD-4D, a temporally resolved robotic CFD benchmark spanning diverse morphologies and flow conditions. To address the computational and autoregressive challenges of this setting, we propose DynaSolver, a neural operator that explicitly conditions on boundary evolution and causal flow history. DynaSolver employs an efficient physical-token formulation that amortizes point-to-token projection across the operator stack, substantially reducing repeated point-space spatio-temporal computation while retaining accurate point-level reconstruction. We further introduce Replay-Augmented Parallel Training, which exposes the model to autoregressively generated histories while preserving parallel dense supervision, narrowing the gap between ground-truth-conditioned training and autoregressive rollout. Experiments on RoboCFD-4D show that DynaSolver achieves the best full-rollout accuracy among a broad range of learned CFD surrogates, with its advantage increasing as rollout proceeds, indicating substantially reduced autoregressive error accumulation. Project page: https://made-gpt.github.io/DynaSolver-ProjectPage.

papers.title: Variational Functional Neural Networks (vfNN)
papers.abstract: We present a variational functional neural network (vfNN) algorithm that optimizes physically motivated continuum functionals in integral form (e.g., Lagrangian, Hamiltonian, or free energy) to find the states of a system. That way, vfNN bypasses solving the equations of motion (a.k.a. the Euler-Lagrange equations), which are in the form of differential equations. To this end, our approach is fundamentally different from conventional physics-informed neural networks (PINN) that solve differential equations by minimizing a phenomenological loss function involving higher order derivatives and ad hoc weight factors. In contrast, vfNN merely evaluates lower order derivatives of the generating functional and replaces the weight factors with rigorous physical scales. This also fundamentally changes the loss landscape, and the desired solutions may become unstable. For this emergent nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a quasi-Newton optimization algorithm with simulated annealing that converges to the solutions of the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations of the functional regardless of their stability properties. Our simulations using vfNN give accurate results for benchmark systems governed by linear or nonlinear ordinary differential equations.

papers.title: When Robots Outweigh Objects: How Inertia Mismatch Shapes Robot Policy Learning
papers.abstract: Conventional robot arms can be extremely heavy compared with the everyday objects they manipulate, creating a significant inertia mismatch at contact. Even a small accidental bump from a heavy arm can knock a light object out of place. Modern learning methods have nevertheless demonstrated a wide range of successful manipulation behaviors on these platforms, suggesting that even extreme inertia mismatch can be overcome with sufficient data. However, it remains unclear whether high inertia imposes a hidden cost on learning, potentially worsening scaling with data or lowering the performance ceiling of modern robot learning methods. We investigate this question through controlled simulation experiments that vary robot and object masses. We find that reinforcement learning succeeds across a broad range of mass combinations, while behavior cloning learns more reliable policies when a lighter robot manipulates a heavier object, and more data narrows the resulting gap without closing it. Behavior cloning likewise degrades on a simulated robot arm as its motors reflect more inertia through their gearing, even though its weight stays the same. Finally, because new hardware is rarely an option, we explore ways to lower contact inertia on the arm one already has, either by choosing a lower-inertia workspace before collecting data or by steering the demonstrator toward lower-inertia solutions of the task. In both simulated cases, the lower-inertia demonstrations are imitated more reliably. Project website: https://younghyopark.me/inertia-mismatch/

papers.title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
papers.abstract: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.

papers.title: Fracture-Bench: A Controlled Benchmark Suite for Machine Learning Surrogates in Phase-Field Fracture Mechanics
papers.abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly proposed to replace phase-field fracture simulations in many-query tasks such as uncertainty quantification, inverse analysis and design. Little controlled evidence shows which architectures are reliable, for which fracture problems and how far beyond their training data. We introduce Fracture-Bench, an open benchmark of two phase-field datasets with fixed splits, common test metrics and a description of each dataset's physical regime. Dataset~1 contains 1,000 AT2 simulations of multiple cracks growing from a notched hole in a hyperelastic plate under random non-uniform biaxial boundary displacements (44 load steps, $128\times128$ grid). Dataset~2 contains 4,000 PF-CZM simulations of a pre-cracked plate with two inclusions, each ten times stiffer or more compliant than the matrix ($128\times256$ grid). We train a Fourier neural operator (FNO), DeepONet, Latent DeepONet, a UNet and a conditional diffusion model on identical splits and compare one test metric per dataset, training time, inference time and model size. On Dataset~1, FNO and Latent DeepONet attain mean test errors of order $10^{-6}$, about ten times lower than UNet and DeepONet. On Dataset~2, the diffusion model is most accurate, with about one sixth of the UNet error, but requires \SI{706}{s} per prediction versus \SI{6}{ms} for UNet. For all architectures, most of the error occurs in the final load steps, after crack localization. Dataset~2 contains initial cracks less than one grid cell apart that produce qualitatively different paths. Architecture rankings therefore depend on the task, and errors averaged over densely sampled inputs reveal little about near-bifurcation cases. Data, codes, splits, regime descriptors and generalization splits are public, with a protocol for adding under-represented regimes such as mixed-mode, three-dimensional and experimentally paired fracture.

papers.title: A Bayesian Framework for Safe Optimal Control of Unknown Systems from Input-Output Data
papers.abstract: As control engineering is applied to increasingly complex systems, learning-based control, which uses empirical data to reduce the reliance on first-principles models, has emerged as a promising paradigm. However, such approaches must cope with nonlinear and stochastic dynamics, the absence of state measurements, and scarce data, while ensuring safe operation under constraints, which requires rigorous uncertainty quantification. Whereas existing methods treat these challenges in isolation, this article proposes a Bayesian framework that jointly addresses them. A prior in state-space form is updated from input-output data using particle Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, yielding a representation of joint uncertainty over dynamics and latent states. Building on this representation, a validation procedure is developed that provides probabilistic guarantees for constraint satisfaction under arbitrary causal control laws. For control synthesis, a formulation penalizing the conditional value-at-risk of the constraint function is proposed, together with an adaptive calibration mechanism that adjusts the performance-robustness trade-off to achieve a desired robustness level. The probability of successful certification is characterized theoretically. The framework is extended to a receding-horizon setting, where posterior updates from new measurements allow the controller to progressively reduce uncertainty and improve performance. The approach is demonstrated on the optimal control of a vertical farm.

papers.title: Toward Uncertainty-Aware, Physics-Grounded Human World Models
papers.abstract: A robot that acts around people needs a world model of the human: a belief over the person's body state and a dynamics model that predicts where that state goes next. This abstract argues that two published components form exactly these two halves, and specifies how to couple them. KNOWN [1] reconstructs the 3D human body while estimating both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in real time (11.6 ms per frame); its aleatoric term identifies unreliable observations, its epistemic term identifies inputs from low-density regions of the training data, and refinement driven by the epistemic term reduces the error on such inputs from 81.3 to 70.3 mm. PhysMoP [2] predicts future body configuration by solving the Euler-Lagrange equations of the body with learned dynamics terms, reducing the 80 ms prediction error from 9.6 to 2.1 mm on Human3.6M and from 12.1 to 0.7 mm on 3DPW. We define the interface between the two, propose three mechanisms by which KNOWN's uncertainty enters PhysMoP, and specify an evaluation protocol on in-the-wild video. No new experimental results are reported here.

papers.title: Policy Iteration over Terminal Cost Functions: From LQR to MPC
papers.abstract: Policy iteration is a classical method for successively improving control policies in optimal control and reinforcement learning. In this paper, we propose a policy iteration framework that refines receding-horizon control (RHC) and model predictive control (MPC) policies online by iteratively updating the terminal cost. We first develop the framework for the linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problem. We show that the Riccati map is a contraction in the Thompson metric on an explicitly constructed invariant order interval. Using this property, we prove convergence of approximate policy iteration for finite-horizon RHC, where the terminal cost is given by an approximate value function. From an initial terminal cost, we then construct a robust invariant order interval within which the RHC policy is refined online. We extend the analysis to constrained MPC and present a constructive algorithm for safely updating the terminal ingredients, which guarantees recursive feasibility and asymptotic stability of the closed loop throughout the iterations. These results connect classical Riccati theory with approximate policy iteration and provide a principled pathway toward learning MPC terminal ingredients. A numerical example illustrates the proposed method.

papers.title: A Geometry-Informed Neural Operator surrogate of LISFLOOD-FP for rapid pluvial-fluvial flood forecasting: the case of Forlì, Italy
papers.abstract: Physically based two-dimensional hydraulic models are too slow for real-time inundation forecasting and large ensembles. We present a time-dependent geometry-informed neural operator (GINO) surrogate of LISFLOOD-FP for the municipality of Forlì (Italy), severely affected by the May 2023 Emilia-Romagna floods. The surrogate is designed for an operational setting in which only river stage gauges and rain gauges are available. A reproducible pipeline turns public regional observations into a physically based training set: each river inflow is driven by the first stage gauge downstream of it through a calibrated water-surface boundary condition, and rain enters as SCS-CN effective rainfall. The surrogate is an autoregressive GINO trained on 216 simulations of 24 observed events with scaled forcing. It predicts volume-conserving polygon-mean depths on an exposure-based Voronoi mesh of 659 nodes, with a 20 min step over 72 h. The surrogate is tested on 38 independent observed events that it never saw during training. On these events it reaches a critical success index (CSI) of 0.934 at 0.05m and 0.844 at 0.3 m, a depth RMSE of 0.008m and an $R^2$ of 0.984 for maximum-depth maps. On one NVIDIA A10G GPU a 72-h forecast takes 1.7 s instead of 55 s with LISFLOOD-FP, and a 50-member ensemble, computed in a single batched rollout, takes 6.2 s instead of about 46 min, which makes probabilistic flood forecasting practical. These results show that neural-operator surrogates can deliver accurate pluvial-fluvial flood forecasts driven by river stage for operational early warning.

papers.title: Safe-Ballbot: Tilt-Consistent MPC with Control Barrier Functions for Ballbot Navigation
papers.abstract: Ball-balancing robots (ballbots) must lean to accelerate, and the lean is limited by the wheel torques and by safety. Planners that use the full robot model are expensive, while planners that ignore the balance dynamics produce references that cannot be followed. This paper presents a two-layer navigation scheme for a three-omni-wheel ballbot. The upper layer is a model predictive controller on a \emph{jerk model} of the ball position, with discrete-time control barrier functions for static, moving, rotating and concave obstacles. The lower layer is a hierarchical sliding mode controller with an extended state observer and a robust exponential control barrier function on the tilt (HSMC-ESO-ECBF). The layers are linked by an acceleration bound derived in closed form from the largest steady tilt that the barrier function admits, so that the plan never asks for a lean the tracker refuses. For obstacles whose motion is only predicted, the obstacles are inflated by conformal prediction radii that bound the prediction error with a prescribed probability. In MuJoCo, with omni-wheel roller contacts and torque saturation, the scheme keeps at least $10$\,cm of clearance, tracks the plan within $2$\,cm RMS, keeps the tilt below the limit and plans in $9$--$12$\,ms, $10$--$15$ times faster than a full-model nonlinear MPC that enters the inflated obstacles; with predicted obstacles, the conformal inflation removes the collisions of a constant-velocity predictor in $30$ random crossing scenarios and reduces them in an endless run on a closed path.The source code and video illustrations are available at https://safe-ballbot.github.io

papers.title: ForceLDM: A Force-aware Latent Dynamics Model for Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires fine-grained control and complex physical interactions with the environment, posing significant challenges for robot policy learning. Vision-only policies struggle with such tasks, as contact states and interaction forces are difficult to infer from visual observations alone. Existing methods mitigate this issue by incorporating force or tactile sensing. However, they often treat these signals as auxiliary observations without fully exploiting their role in modeling future interaction dynamics. To address this, we propose ForceLDM, a force-aware latent dynamics model that learns future contact and motion dynamics to guide action generation. Rather than directly predicting future observations, which can entangle task-relevant dynamics with irrelevant sensory details, ForceLDM learns a compact representation of future dynamics through knowledge distillation. Specifically, a teacher network with privileged future force/torque and optical flow signals extracts future dynamic features, which are then distilled into a student network trained only on current observations. This enables the student model to reason about upcoming contacts and physical dynamics without relying on future sensory inputs at deployment. To improve robustness and generalization, we further introduce a curriculum-based progressive noise injection strategy to mitigate over-reliance on future features. Experiments on five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks demonstrate that ForceLDM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, generalizes effectively to novel objects, and remains robust to environmental perturbations. Project page and code are available at https://tpy001.github.io/ForceLDM/.

papers.title: DeepWaveRL: Self-Supervised Full Waveform Inversion via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) is a fundamental inverse problem in geophysics to estimate subsurface properties, such as velocity, from seismic measurements. Recently, self-supervised learning methods remove the need for ground-truth velocity maps during training by leveraging a forward operator to simulate seismic data from predictions and backpropagate the gradients of reconstruction loss through it. In this work, we consider a more challenging setting without accessing such gradients. To this end, we incorporate reinforcement learning into self-supervised FWI and propose a framework named DeepWaveRL. Specifically, we reformulate FWI as a policy learning problem, where the policy network predicts velocity maps as actions, and a forward operator is used solely for simulation. A global scalar reward is computed based on data misfit for each prediction and used to weight policy gradients. Thus, learning proceeds without accessing the gradients from the forward operator. Given the indirect and coarse supervision signals, we further identify key strategies to stabilize learning and mitigate the spatial credit assignment bottleneck. Experimental results show that, despite relying entirely on a single scalar reward, DeepWaveRL achieves competitive performance compared to supervised and self-supervised baselines. These findings suggest that our framework offers a flexible and complementary learning paradigm for the FWI research community.

papers.title: From PID to Reinforcement Learning in Building HVAC Control: A Control-Architecture Review of Tuning Strategies, Formulations, and Deployment Trade-offs
papers.abstract: This paper reviews control architectures for building heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems, addressing the tension among energy demand, occupant comfort and equipment operability, and situating proportional-integral-derivative (PID) regulation within a layered control stack that also includes rule-based and model-based supervisory control and data-driven reinforcement learning (RL). It examines the thermostat-PID layer from two-position and scheduled setpoint control through proportional, PI and PID regulation and their tuning, then formulates RL for building control as a Markov decision process. Its central contribution is a taxonomy of where RL meets PID: RL as a gain tuner for an existing loop, as a direct replacement for the regulatory controller, as a hybrid with model predictive control, and as supervisory setpoint and schedule generation. Across these classes, the review establishes that the physical loop remains invariant while the intervention point changes, and that the classes differ in their requirements for actuation authority, state information, modelling, commissioning and constraint handling. It further establishes that PID is inexpensive and well codified but limited by nonlinearity, time variation, discrete mode switching, loop interaction and slow plant dynamics, while RL's admissible position must be argued rather than assumed. The paper concludes that these architectures are not competing philosophies of control but nested points of attachment on one HVAC plant, with hybrid implementations possible, and that deployment trade-offs must be assessed according to the specific control interface and scaffolding required.

papers.title: KlaskTron: An Open-Source Platform for Physical Adversarial Multi-Agent RL
papers.abstract: Progress in robot learning, particularly physical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), is currently challenged by a limited availability of accessible, standardized benchmarks. While simulation-based MARL has produced remarkable emergent behaviors, from coordinated team play to complex tool use, translating these advances to physical systems remains difficult. A key barrier is infrastructural: physical platforms are often prohibitively expensive, require specialized facilities, or lack open mechanisms and designs for reproducibility. We introduce KlaskTron, an open-source, low-cost (<\$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed for adversarial MARL based on the dynamic tabletop game KLASK. The platform features dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors, enabling the high-speed, precise manipulation required for competitive play. Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].

Under poor illumination, MISLAM maintains tracking after visual-inertial odometry fails, achieving a horizontal closure error of 0.332 m, although vertical drift remains a limitation. The extension uses experimentally identified airflow models to compute the forces and torques exerted on objects. To enable physical execution, we design a lightweight, high-speed blower that coexists with a gripper. In zero-shot real-world deployment, HPB achieves an 80% success rate over 20 trials, while RR achieves a mean absolute heading error of 2.6 degrees across four target headings. papers.abstract: Autonomous inspection of a resident space object is usually posed as a contest between classical next-best-view planning and reinforcement learning. On a controlled ladder in which one design axis is varied at a time, fuel efficiency turns out to be set by three things: whether the agent is allowed to drift, whether its state records where drifting has taken it, and whether its planning horizon is long enough for the benefit to appear. Removing any one of them doubles the fuel bill or more. The algorithm still matters, but through what it can represent: a model-based agent whose learned world model ignores fuel spends several times more of it. Finally, no learned policy is safe by construction, and a control barrier function filter beneath the decision layer removed every keep-out-zone violation in two thousand evaluation episodes.

As established by a rationality theorem, the operator captures a directed interventional response at each brain state, and under invariance assumptions the operator is identifiable from data, with its signed output separating excitatory from inhibitory influences. On synthetic benchmarks, \model recovers the causal structure on Lorenz96 and achieves the lowest mean structural Hamming distance among compared methods on NetSim, while preserving signed influence structures that distinguish excitatory from inhibitory interactions. We address this with an LLM-based narrative platform whose managers are interchangeable modules operating over a shared symbolic world model of facts, operations, and goals. papers.title: POD-CNF: reduced order modeling of parametrized stochastic PDEs via normalizing flows and proper orthogonal decomposition
papers.abstract: Reduced-order models (ROMs) learned from trusted numerical simulations enable the real-time simulation of complex physical systems, making computationally prohibitive tasks-such as uncertainty quantification and optimal control-tractable. In particular, data-driven ROMs are opening the opportunity to learn from both numerical simulations and experimental data. However, integrating these sources of information is far from straightforward. Real-world measurements often involve multiple sources of uncertainty, including non-Gaussian noise, latent heterogeneities, unknown or hidden system parameters, and multiscale phenomena occurring below the resolution of the data. Consequently, real-world data are better described by parametrized stochastic partial differential equations, for which the development of effective ROMs remains relatively unexplored. In this work, we introduce POD-CNF, a data-driven generative ROM for efficient uncertainty quantification of parametrized high-dimensional systems. The approach combines projection-based model reduction and deep generative modeling. First, Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) is employed to obtain a low-dimensional representation of the solution manifold. A Conditional Normalizing Flow (CNF) is then trained to approximate the density of the reduced coefficients conditionally on the input parameters. This formulation allows the surrogate to capture complex, multimodal output distributions, going beyond standard regression-based ROMs and least-squares predictions. We assess the effectiveness of POD-CNF through numerical experiments, demonstrating its ability to accurately reproduce output distributions while substantially reducing computational costs. Finally, a proof-of-concept application illustrates how the generative paradigm facilitates integration into Bayesian inverse problems, highlighting promising directions for future research.

papers.title: The Staged Pandora's Box: Reservation Indices for Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization
papers.abstract: A staged search must decide which candidate to advance next and when to stop. Some observations only inform later decisions; others can be kept as results. We formulate these choices as a staged Pandora's box with a designated set of collectable stages. For independent finite-stage candidates with bounded readings and positive bounded own-history costs, an exact covered-call recursion gives the reservation index, the optimal value and the loss of every advance or stop; advancing an index-maximal candidate while its index exceeds the incumbent is optimal. The representation recovers classical single-stage search, nested inspection and the all-collectable Markov setting, and prices changes in the problem: enlarging the collectable set or lowering costs raises the value by an explicit covered-call overshoot. Resumption can be valuable even when future reward laws do not change, but has no value for deterministic readings. With information sharing across candidates, no rule using only their separate remaining-reading laws is universally optimal, and making an intermediate reading collectable can change which candidate is inspected first. Under a coherent joint path law with own-history costs, an approximate-planning bound controls the recomputed index's regret by changes in untouched candidates' local values; a common-component specialization bounds those changes through predictive total-variation dispersion. Exact finite-law experiments check the representation, the loss accounting and the bounds.

Dynamic expectations and new observations jointly inform the current estimate, which in turn anchors personalized forecasts based on shared knowledge and individual experience. An external policy relates forecasts under alternative conditions to the person's goals, preferences, and constraints when considering support. Actual responses and outcomes provide evidence for revising the state estimate and personal dynamic patterns, thereby informing subsequent estimation, prediction, and support. We illustrate the framework through hypothetical training and learning scenarios. Our research agenda asks whether accumulated interaction experience improves subsequent estimation and prediction, and whether using the model helps the person pursue their goals over time.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents are vulnerable to perturbations of their observed state inputs. Prior works often constrain state adversaries with $L_p$-norm uncertainty sets and evaluate policy performance under the resulting perturbations. However, in continuous control tasks like robotics control, different state dimensions have distinct physical meanings and influence policy behavior to different degrees, which $L_p$-norm sets fail to capture or explain. Moreover, it is important to identify when and along which state dimensions a policy is vulnerable, independently of the algorithm used to train it. In this paper, we focus on evaluation-time attacks applied to pretrained policies. We propose \textbf{P}erformance-\textbf{D}egradation \textbf{N}on-\textbf{U}niform \textbf{U}ncertainty \textbf{S}et (\method{}), an interpretable formulation of uncertainty sets for state perturbations. \method{} is state-dependent, dimension-wise non-uniform, and can be synthesized online during policy evaluation. We first formulate an ideal constrained optimization problem for \method{} computation, then introduce a surrogate constraint to make the problem tractable. Experiments across multiple continuous-control environments, policy algorithms, and state attacks show that \method{} reveals variation in policy sensitivity across states and dimensions, while its performance degradation is moderately controlled.

papers.title: INTERACT: Learning Interaction-Aware World Dynamics from Driving Videos for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Safe autonomous driving requires more than recognizing the current scene: the ego vehicle must anticipate how surrounding traffic participants will evolve under its own motion. However, existing end-to-end driving models typically encode scenes into dense visual or BEV features, leaving object-level interactions implicit. We propose (INTERACT INTERaction-aware Action-Conditioned Trajectory learning), a three-stage framework that learns a slot-based object-centric world model from unlabeled driving videos and transfers it to trajectory planning. INTERACT first learns recurrent slots that group dense visual features into temporally structured scene-entity representations without object annotations. It then infers latent ego actions from slot context and video transitions, and uses them to condition future slot prediction, capturing how ego motion and surrounding entities co-evolve. Finally, the learned slots, latent actions, and future slot predictions are distilled into a trajectory planner to guide trajectory generation and selection. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM and nuScenes validate the effectiveness of INTERACT. In particular, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM, with improvements in safety-critical collision metrics.

papers.title: End-to-End Stability of Online Active Learning in Large-Scale Neural Systems
papers.abstract: Online Active Learning (OAL) aims to extend deep learning from static inference after offline training to continuous adaptation during real-time interaction with a changing physical environment. This transition is essential for safety-critical applications, but it raises a central theoretical question: whether the online parameter update process remains stable when scaled to multilayer neural architectures. This paper develops a stability-focused OAL framework. The framework uses prediction error as a feedback signal to update a structured deep model, thereby linking online learning with Lyapunov-based energy minimization. We show that prediction error convergence alone is insufficient for global parameter convergence because multilayer networks may admit high-dimensional manifolds of equivalent output solutions. The analysis therefore separates output error regulation, internal zero dynamics, interlayer coupling, and parameter convergence. Persistency of excitation and active damping are then used to remove the residual null-space modes that remain after output error convergence. A cascaded Lyapunov analysis establishes asymptotic stability of the overall OAL learning process, while monotonic activation functions and diffeomorphic layer mappings provide the uniqueness condition for the target parameter trajectory. The resulting proof provides a theoretical basis for applying online adaptive learning to large-scale neural systems in nonstationary and safety-critical settings.

papers.title: Learning Purposeful Co-designs of Bio-inspired Quadrupedal Robots
papers.abstract: Treating morphology and control as separate design problems has constrained the efficiency and adaptability of quadrupedal robots, while current co-design approaches are often constrained by restricted design spaces. We overcome this limit by introducing Dogger, a bio-inspired quadruped with modular three-segment legs, four-bar linkages and adjustable passive knee compliance. A two-stage framework combining reinforcement learning and Bayesian optimization is developed: the morphology-conditioned control policy is trained across designs and then held fixed during task-specific design selection. The resulting designs and policies deployed zero-shot reduce the cost of transport by 18.6% and 35.7% for inspection and payload-carrying tasks. Comparisons demonstrate that full geometry-compliance co-design outperforms fixed and restricted design scopes. Cross-task tests further reveal distinct task-specific morphologies with shared mechanical trade-offs. These results provide hardware-level evidence that expanding the physical design space alongside learned control is essential to realize the full potential of task-driven morphology-control co-design in legged robotics.

papers.title: Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision for Replica-Exchange Training of Geometry-Aware Neural Operators with Uncertainty Quantification
papers.abstract: Geometry-aware neural operators face substantial computational and memory demands when learning across complex physical domains. We introduce Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision (AA-MP), a replica-exchange training strategy that allocates numerical precision according to replica roles and architecture-specific operations. By retaining FP32 for refinement while selectively employing BF16 for exploration, AA-MP preserves predictive accuracy while improving training efficiency. Across fluid dynamics and three-dimensional structural mechanics benchmarks, AA-MP achieves comparable accuracy to full-precision training over an ensemble of runs, while reducing hot-replica peak GPU memory by 46.9% and training time by up to 25.8%. It also outperforms naive Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) in memory efficiency and computational cost, with increasing memory advantages at larger model and geometry scales. Ablation studies show that retaining FP32 in the cold-replica is important for predictive accuracy, while additional FP32 operations in the exploratory replica provide limited benefits relative to their computational cost. Finally, conformal prediction for uncertainty calibration shows that AA-MP achieves near-nominal coverage with narrower prediction intervals than the alternatives. These results advance the scalability of geometry-aware scientific machine learning by reducing computational costs without compromising predictive accuracy or uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: MirrorComm: A Communication-Efficient Cooperative Perception Framework via Mirrored World Models
papers.abstract: Cooperative perception (CP) requires substantial communication bandwidth to exchange sensing information among connected agents. A variety of compression techniques have been proposed to reduce transmission costs while retaining task-relevant information. However, most existing methods follow a frame-wise compression paradigm, overlooking temporal predictability and repeatedly transmitting information that could be inferred from historical context. To address these limitations, we propose MirrorComm, the first world model-based communication-efficient CP framework. Specifically, mirrored world models at the transmitter and receiver predict the transmitter's current observation from a shared history of its reconstructed observations. The transmitter compares this prediction with its current observation and selectively transmits observation updates to correct prediction errors, reducing repeated transmission of predictable information. Experiments on the OPV2V dataset across two downstream tasks including object detection and semantic segmentation show that MirrorComm reduces communication bandwidth requirements by up to approximately 66-fold while maintaining comparable performance to a state-of-the-art (SOTA) method. Ablation studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of the individual components.

papers.title: AgiWorld: An Agentic Video World Model for Building Persistent Worlds
papers.abstract: Recent interactive video world models generate visually compelling videos from a single image, following user-provided camera motion and text prompts. However, such low-level control demands substantial user effort to realize a high-level intent, and the generated world struggles to remain persistent as the exploration proceeds. In this work, we present AgiWorld, an agentic video world model that explores and builds a persistent world from a single image and a free-form instruction. For high-level planning, our agent AgiWorld-Agent designs the world and the journey through it in a world state and directs the exploration. For low-level realization, our video world model AgiWorld-WM generates the video chunk by chunk and stores it with its geometry in a spatial memory, from which the agent updates its world state. This closed loop keeps the world faithful to the user's intent and keeps the agent's world state consistent with the generated content throughout the exploration. We co-design the two levels around the shared spatial memory and an interface of metric camera trajectories and structured prompts. In AgiWorld-WM, to handle occlusion and accumulated geometric errors in the spatial memory over long rollouts, we propose occlusion-aware history selection, which retrieves past views by surface visibility, and reliability-based memory maintenance, which prefers reliable geometry and earlier observations. AgiWorld-WM achieves state-of-the-art overall performance on world revisiting and exploration benchmarks, and qualitative results and ablations show that AgiWorld builds persistent worlds from free-form instructions over minute-long journeys. Persistence thus arises not from the video model alone but from its closed loop with the agent.

papers.title: Functional Outcomes Following Cemented Bipolar Hemiarthroplasty Versus Total Hip Arthroplasty for Displaced Femoral Neck Fractures in Older Adults: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Background: Older persons frequently sustain femoral neck fractures, which are linked to significant morbidity and functional loss. Although total hip arthroplasty (THA) and cemented bipolar hemiarthroplasty (CBH) are common treatment choices, there is ongoing debate regarding which is better. Methodology: The Department of Orthopaedics at Arif Memorial Teaching Hospital carried out a retrospective cohort analysis. Included were eighty patients 60 years of age or older who had either THA (n = 40) or CBH (n = 40). One year following surgery, the Modified Harris Hip Score was used to evaluate the functional result. The two groups were also compared in terms of postoperative recuperation, complications, patient satisfaction, and quality of life. Results: Except for body weight, which was considerably higher in the THA group (p = 0.044), the two groups' baseline clinical and demographic parameters were similar. Postoperative ambulation, discomfort, activities of daily living, return to normal activities, and components of the Modified Harris Hip Score did not differ significantly (all p > 0.05). The THA group experienced greater postoperative problems than the CBH group (17.5% vs. 5.0%), but this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.154). Conclusion: Both CBH and THA provided satisfactory functional outcomes after surgery. No differences were noted in functional recovery between the two techniques, but CBH had a slightly lower but non-significant number of postoperative complications. This study proves the importance of personalized surgical approach according to the patient’s characteristics rather than a bias toward one technique.

papers.abstract: Abstract Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) reconstruction is challenged by graft elongation and delayed biological integration, often necessitating slow rehabilitation and carrying a risk of arthrofibrosis. This technical report describes an all‐inside technique augmented with the modified internal bracing to address these limitations. The technique involves integrating a FiberTape within a quadrupled Achilles tendon allograft, creating a load‐sharing composite. An all‐inside, retrograde socket method was used for anatomic PCL reconstruction in the knee, with suspensory fixation on both femur and tibia. The graft‐tape construct was simultaneously tensioned. The technique provides immediate biomechanical stability by mitigating graft micromotion, elongation, and tunnel abrasion. By closely replicating native PCL stiffness, this construct facilitates an accelerated, protective rehabilitation protocol focused on early motion and quadriceps activation, thereby aiming to reduce failure rates and postoperative stiffness. This method represents a synergistic evolution in PCL reconstruction, combining synthetic reinforcement with biological healing.

papers.title: Early (<3 months) versus late (≥3 months) periprosthetic femoral fractures after hip arthroplasty: fracture characteristics and treatment patterns
papers.abstract: Background To describe and compare injury context, fracture morphology, bone stock, and treatment patterns between periprosthetic femoral fractures (PFFs) occurring <3 months and ≥3 months after index hip arthroplasty using a prespecified operational timing threshold. Methods We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients hospitalized for their first documented PFF episode after total hip arthroplasty or hemiarthroplasty at a tertiary orthopedic referral hospital from January 2021 through December 2025. Early PFF was defined as <3 months and late PFF as ≥3 months using a prespecified primary operational cutoff based on the month-level interval from index arthroplasty to PFF. Between-group comparisons used Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, Fisher exact tests, and standardized mean differences (SMDs). P values were interpreted descriptively, and absolute percentage-point differences with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported for selected binary contrasts. A 6-month cutoff was examined post hoc as a sensitivity analysis. Results Among 132 patients, 126 had a usable month-based interval; 23 (18.3%) had early PFF and 103 (81.7%) had late PFF. Low-energy injury was recorded in 23/23 (100.0%) early PFFs and 86/102 (84.3%) late PFFs, corresponding to an absolute difference of 15.7 percentage points (95% CI, 0.2–24.0). Vancouver B2/B3 fractures occurred in 8/23 (34.8%) versus 22/102 (21.6%) patients (absolute difference, 13.2 percentage points; 95% CI, −5.1–34.7). Surgery was performed in 21/23 (91.3%) versus 88/103 (85.4%), and ORIF was the most frequent treatment in both groups. At the 6-month cutoff, multiple fracture categories and treatment strategies remained represented in both timing groups. Conclusions In this cohort, a 3-month operational grouping suggested a difference in recorded injury context, while both timing groups included multiple fracture morphologies, bone-stock categories, and treatment strategies. Timing may provide useful contextual information at presentation but should be interpreted together with Vancouver classification, implant stability, bone stock, and patient condition. These observations require validation in larger cohorts with finer timing resolution.

papers.title: Process parameter interactions and volumetric energy density Non-Uniqueness in LPBF-Processed CuCrZr alloy: Effects on defect evolution and densification
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the densification behavior and defect evolution of CuCrZr alloy fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), with emphasis on the effects of laser power (LP), scanning speed (SS), hatch distance (HD) and powder bed layer thickness (PBLT) on density, microstructure, defects and mechanical performance. The suitability of volumetric energy density (VED) for predicting densification and defect formation is also evaluated. Design/methodology/approach A statistically validated experimental framework based on a modified Taguchi method was used to optimize the LPBF process parameters. Eighty-one CuCrZr specimens were fabricated under different processing conditions. Density measurements, optical and scanning electron microscopy, defect characterization and mechanical testing were performed to establish process-structure-property relationships and evaluate the effects of post-heat treatment. Findings The optimized parameters of LP = 370 W, SS = 610 mm/s, HD = 0.10 mm and PBLT = 30 µm produced relative density above 99.6% with minimal defects. Lack-of-fusion defects, gas porosity and interlayer cracking were strongly influenced by melting pool behavior and process parameter interactions. Microstructural analysis revealed a transition from fine equiaxed grains to elongated columnar grains along the build direction. Direct aging produced the highest strength, with a yield strength of 435 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 437 MPa, while solution treatment followed by aging increased elongation up to 13%. Originality/value The results demonstrate that VED alone is insufficient for predicting densification because different parameter combinations with similar VED values produced distinct density levels and defect morphologies. The modified Taguchi framework provides a systematic approach for optimizing LPBF parameters and establishing relationships between processing conditions, defects, microstructure and mechanical performance of CuCrZr alloy.

papers.title: 3D bioprinting strategies for dentin–pulp complex regeneration: a systematic review
papers.abstract: Dental pulp injury due to caries, trauma, or restorative procedures may require root canal therapy, which eliminates infected pulp tissue but does not restore the biological functions of the native pulp. Additive manufacturing technologies, including three-dimensional (3D) printing and bioprinting, have emerged as potential approaches for developing biomaterial constructs for dentin–pulp tissue engineering. This systematic review synthesized experimental evidence on additive manufacturing strategies relevant to dentin–pulp complex regeneration, with emphasis on printing approaches, scaffold and bioink materials, and reported biological outcomes. A systematic literature search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection from inception to September 11, 2026. Experimental studies using 3D printing or bioprinting to fabricate constructs intended for dentin, pulp, or the dentin–pulp complex were eligible. Outcomes included odontogenic differentiation, mineralization, vascularization, and tissue formation. Two reviewers independently performed study selection and data extraction, with third-reviewer adjudication when required. Methodological reporting and potential sources of bias were assessed using a six-domain review-specific framework. Owing to substantial heterogeneity in materials, fabrication strategies, experimental models, and outcomes, findings were synthesized narratively. Forty-two experimental studies met the inclusion criteria. Extrusion-based printing was the most frequently used fabrication approach, followed by fused deposition modeling and light-based methods such as stereolithography and digital light processing. Common material systems included polycaprolactone composites, gelatin methacryloyl-based bioinks, and bioactive ceramics. Reported outcomes included odontogenic marker expression, mineralization, vascularization, cell viability, and tissue-level responses in preclinical models. Dentin bridge formation and tertiary dentin deposition in pulp injury models were interpreted as reparative outcomes rather than evidence of complete dentin–pulp complex regeneration. The available evidence supports the biological potential of 3D printing and bioprinting for dentin–pulp tissue engineering, but confidence in the evidence remains limited. Most studies were in vitro or preclinical and showed substantial heterogeneity in fabrication methods, biomaterials, experimental models, outcome measures, and methodological reporting. Further standardized and adequately reported preclinical studies using clinically relevant models and validated outcome measures are needed before predictable clinical regeneration of a functional dentin–pulp complex can be established.

papers.title: FEM Validation of Form-Found Shell Roofs Designed in Seismic Areas
papers.abstract: Abstract Shell structures offer high structural efficiency when their shapes allow loads to be carried mainly through compression, making them particularly suitable for materials with limited tensile strength, such as masonry, unreinforced concrete, and unreinforced 3D-printed concrete. The purpose of this work is to evaluate the structural quality and practical reliability of shells obtained through a physics-informed neural network-based optimized constrained form-finding (PINN-OCFF) methodology. This form-finding approach explicitly accounts for both vertical and horizontal loading conditions at the design stage by identifying an isoresistant volume capable of withstanding these actions through pure compression. Unlike traditional form-finding methods that focus primarily on gravity loading, the PINN-OCFF strategy generates shell shapes intended to remain in compression under combined loading conditions relevant to real design situations. The study focuses on a shell designed through this PINN-OCFF framework and assesses its performance through finite-element method (FEM) analyses carried out in Abaqus, following modeling assumptions commonly adopted in engineering practice and required by design codes such as the Eurocodes, ACI, or the Italian NTC. The FEM results are compared with the membrane equilibrium predicted by the form-finding process in terms of the stress distribution, development of tensile zones, and overall structural response. To investigate the influence of boundary conditions, three different constraint configurations are considered: fully fixed edges, fully hinged edges, and hinges located only at the base supports. For comparison, a shell of uniform thickness is considered and analyzed under the same vertical and horizontal loads used during form finding. The analyses show that the shell designed through the PINN-OCFF form-finding process better preserves compression-dominated behavior under realistic modeling assumptions, even when horizontal loading conditions and nonideal boundary conditions are introduced. Compared to shells designed considering vertical loads alone or employing a uniform thickness, the optimized shell exhibits reduced bending effects and limited tensile stresses. These findings demonstrate that incorporating horizontal actions directly into the form-finding stage leads to more robust and practically reliable shell designs, supporting the use of the PINN-OCFF methodology as an effective preliminary design tool for compression-dominated shell structures.

papers.title: 3D bioprinting of vascularized cardiac constructs reveals improved cardiomyocyte organization and contractile function
papers.abstract: Background Despite advances in cardiac tissue engineering, generating constructs that simultaneously achieve vascularization and organized cardiomyocyte function remains a major challenge. Methods In this study, three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting was used to fabricate human umbilical vein endothelial cell (HUVEC)-laden alginate/gelatin constructs with defined architectures designed to mimic myocardial alignment. Constructs were cultured with vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF) under static conditions followed by short-term dynamic stimulation in a bioreactor. Cardiomyocytes - H9c2 cells, neonatal rat ventricular myocytes (NRVMs), or human induced pluripotent stem cell–derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) - were subsequently seeded onto the constructs. Vascularization and the distribution of cells were assessed using immunofluorescence, and functional activity of cardiomyocytes was evaluated by calcium transient imaging. Results Bioprinted constructs developed interconnected CD31-positive endothelial networks in response to growth factor supplementation and dynamic culture, whereas control constructs cultured without growth factors or bioreactor exposure showed limited vascular organization. Cardiomyocytes seeded onto vascularized constructs exhibited improved structural organization, including increased alignment and integration with endothelial networks. Functional assessment revealed more synchronized and rhythmic calcium transients compared to non-vascularized constructs. Conclusion This study demonstrates that combining 3D bioprinting with controlled architectural design and endothelial network formation enhances cardiomyocyte organization and function. These findings highlight the critical role of vascular-like networks in improving the performance of engineered cardiac tissues.

papers.title: Primary stability of dental implants placed by novice surgeons: an ex vivo study across two implant systems in a porcine mandible model
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose Dental implant placement is a technically demanding procedure in which surgical experience is considered a key determinant of outcome. Primary stability, as measured by the implant stability quotient (ISQ) via resonance frequency analysis (RFA), is a critical predictor of successful osseointegration. This study aimed to quantify the influence of surgical experience on primary implant stability in a standardized porcine mandible model. Methods Dental students with no prior implant experience and experienced oral surgeons placed implants using two commercially available systems (Straumann Standard Plus and Astra Tech EV). Primary stability was assessed by RFA immediately after insertion at four standardized measurement positions. ISQ values were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model with surgical experience, implant system, and measurement position as fixed factors and a random intercept for implant to account for the non-independence of the four measurements obtained per implant. Results A total of 760 ISQ measurements were included in the analysis. Experienced surgeons achieved significantly higher ISQ values (M = 75.72, SD = 5.22) than students (M = 68.68, SD = 11.61; p < 0.001), with an overall mean difference of approximately 7 ISQ points. Within the Straumann Standard Plus, the difference was 8.14 ISQ points ( p = 0.028); within the Astra Tech EV, the difference was 5.42 ISQ points ( p < 0.001). Variability was markedly greater in the student group across both systems. Conclusions Surgical experience significantly influences primary implant stability within both implant systems investigated. Novice operators achieve lower and less consistent ISQ values, which may have clinical implications for the selection of loading protocols. These findings suggest that structured training may help improve primary stability among less-experienced operators, a hypothesis that warrants prospective clinical evaluation. papers.title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Postoperative Complications Using Laboratory and Clinical Parameters in Total Hip and Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Scoping Review
papers.abstract: Background: Total joint arthroplasties (TJAs) are well-established orthopedic procedures that provide effective pain relief and restore functional mobility. Although these procedures are generally highly successful, postoperative complications may still occur. This review examined the literature on how machine learning (ML) can predict postoperative complications based on laboratory and clinical parameters for total knee (TKA) and total hip arthroplasty (THA). Methods: A scoping review was conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA criteria for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR). We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and EMBASE for studies evaluating the use of ML to predict adverse events following TKA and/or THA, using routinely available laboratory values combined with demographics and clinical parameters. Results: The initial search yielded 144 studies, of which 18 were finally deemed eligible for inclusion. Key predictors of complications in the examined studies included hemoglobin, hematocrit, white blood cell count, platelet count, and renal markers. Need for transfusion was the most frequently studied outcome, followed by severe adverse events and postoperative delirium. The ML models, especially gradient boosting machines (GBMs), random forests (RFs), and neural networks (NNs), demonstrated promising discriminative performance in predicting adverse events. Conclusions: Combining laboratory data with demographics and clinical information may improve the accuracy of complication prediction. This review emphasizes the potential of ML analysis of laboratory parameters to create risk assessment tools, which could detect complication risk and potentially improve outcomes for patients undergoing TKA or THA.

papers.title: Predictive control method for aero-engine life extension considering combustion chamber outlet temperature distribution
papers.abstract: Abstract Nonuniform combustor-exit temperature distribution can induce local hot spots on turbine blades, increase thermal gradients, and accelerate thermomechanical fatigue damage. Conventional aero-engine control optimization mainly focuses on thrust and fuel consumption, with limited consideration of component service life. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a life-extending model predictive control method for turbofan engines that accounts for combustor-exit temperature distribution. CFD simulations are first conducted to characterize the outlet temperature distribution under different operating conditions. A prediction model that combines a deep neural network with a state-variable model is constructed to meet the requirements of online optimization. The resulting nonlinear optimization problem is then reformulated as a quadratic programming problem. Validation results show that the maximum dynamic prediction error is 4.35 %, indicating sufficient accuracy for online predictive control. For the PLA transition from 20° to 70°, the proposed method reduces the peak turbine-inlet hot-spot temperature by 32 K and increases the predicted thermomechanical-fatigue safe life of the high-pressure turbine guide vane by 19.3 % compared with the conventional LEC method.

papers.title: Quantum theory of electrically levitated nanoparticle-ion systems: Motional dynamics and sympathetic cooling
papers.abstract: We develop the theory describing the quantum coupled dynamics of the center-of-mass motion of a nanoparticle and an ensemble of ions co-trapped in a dual-frequency linear Paul trap. We first derive analytical expressions for the motional frequencies and classical trajectories of both nanoparticle and ions. We then derive a quantum master equation for the ion-nanoparticle system and quantify the sympathetic cooling of the nanoparticle motion enabled by its Coulomb coupling to a continuously Doppler-cooled ion. We predict that motional cooling down to sub-kelvin temperatures is achievable in state-of-the-art experiments even in the absence of motional feedback and in the presence of micromotion. We then extend our analysis to an ensemble of $N$ ions, predicting a linear increase of the cooling rate as a function of $N$ and motional cooling of the nanoparticle down to tenths of millikelvin in current experimental platforms. Our work establishes the theoretical toolbox needed to explore the ion-assisted preparation of non-Gaussian motional states of levitated nanoparticles.

papers.title: Technical note: Benefits of Bayesian estimation of model parameters in a large hydrological model ensemble
papers.abstract: Abstract. Quantifying and mitigating parametric and structural uncertainties in hydrological models are crucial to accurately understand and predict the rainfall-runoff process. Despite recent advances in Bayesian approaches for quantifying structural uncertainty using very large hydrological model ensembles, the simultaneous quantification of both parametric and structural uncertainties has yet to be implemented since previous works on large model ensembles have relied on deterministic optimization of parameters. Here we present the potential benefits of Bayesian estimation of parametric uncertainty within a large hydrological model ensemble. We find that Bayesian estimation of model parameters (more generally, change in calibration methods) potentially influences the interpretation of model comparisons. Specifically, Bayesian parametric uncertainty quantification greatly benefits complex models with many parameters, thereby affecting discussions of the appropriate level of model complexity. We also find that Bayesian parametric uncertainty quantification does not substantially improve multi-model hydrological predictions. The adverse effects of parameter misspecification in individual models are effectively mitigated by combining models with diverse structures. Thus, the high computational cost of Bayesian parameter estimation is not paid for to improve rainfall-runoff analysis in a large hydrological model ensemble.

papers.title: Multifidelity Aerodynamic Data Fusion by Autoencoder Transfer Learning
papers.abstract: Accurate aerodynamic prediction often relies on high-fidelity (HF) simulations; however, their prohibitive computational costs severely limit their applicability in data-driven modeling. This limitation motivates the development of multifidelity strategies that leverage inexpensive low-fidelity (LF) information without compromising accuracy. Addressing this challenge, this work presents a multifidelity deep learning framework that combines autoencoder-based transfer learning with a newly developed multisplit conformal prediction (MSCP) strategy to achieve uncertainty-aware aerodynamic data fusion under extreme data scarcity. The methodology leverages abundant LF data to learn a compact latent physics representation, which acts as a frozen knowledge base for a decoder that is subsequently fine-tuned using scarce HF samples. Tested on surface-pressure distributions for NACA airfoils (two-dimensional) and a transonic wing (three-dimensional) databases, the model successfully corrects LF deviations and achieves high-accuracy pressure predictions using minimal HF training data. Furthermore, the MSCP framework produces robust, actionable uncertainty bands with pointwise coverage exceeding 95%. By combining extreme data efficiency with uncertainty quantification, this work offers a scalable and reliable solution for aerodynamic regression in data-scarce environments.

papers.title: Predicting East Africa’s rainfall extremes with calibrated AI post-processing systems
papers.abstract: Abstract Accurate and reliable rainfall forecasts are crucial for Early Warning Systems (EWS). Artificial Intelligence approaches, which post-process global physical forecasts, enable low-cost ensemble generation, extending skill to medium-range lead times and offering scalable systems to inform EWS particularly under resource-constrained settings. However, assessing their practical value in representing user-relevant rainfall extremes and guiding decisions for EWS remains critical. We present a low-cost, uncertainty quantification method that calibrates ensemble forecasts to probabilities of exceedances for rainfall extremes. Applied to raw and post-processed rainfall forecasts over East Africa, sub-regional analysis shows the threshold-calibrated, post-processed forecasts better reflecting the observed chances of extremes at higher rainfall thresholds. Case-study results show encouraging added value from post-processed forecasts at longer lead times. Forecast skill decomposed across rainfall and probability thresholds highlights the ranges of rainfall and risk tolerances where most actionable improvement arises, whether using satellite or rain-gauge data as reference. This tailored evaluation helps guide forecast adoption for EWS.

papers.title: Design of Monolithic Microcavities for Enhancing Organic Quantum Emitters
papers.abstract: Abstract Single organic molecules are a well-established platform for high-quality single-photon generation: they can emit lifetime-limited photons with high purity and indistinguishability. However, their emission is accompanied by a pronounced red-shifted phonon sideband and higher-order vibrational peaks, which reduce the fraction of photons emitted into the desired narrowband zero-phonon line. The standard approach to suppressing this unwanted emission is to integrate the emitter into a monolithic photonic nanostructure that provides Purcell enhancement. However, incorporating organic materials using clean-room techniques has proven challenging and has, in fact, so far prevented the integration of single molecules in crystalline hosts into monolithic microcavities. As a result, efficient, narrowband organic single-photon sources for applications in quantum information processing have remained elusive despite their considerable promise. Here, we propose three monolithic microcavity designs tailored to provide sufficient Purcell enhancement for organic quantum emitters. The Purcell effect induced by these cavities preferentially enhances emission into the 0–0 zero-phonon line, increasing spectral purity, photon extraction, and shortening the excited-state lifetime, which in turn relaxes the requirements for generating indistinguishable photons. The cavities have been optimized using Bayesian optimization and the adaptive Antoulas–Anderson (AAA) algorithm for rational approximation, which offer global optimization and the efficient reconstruction of spectra from scattering simulations, respectively. These structures are compatible with both standard clean-room processing and single-molecule preparation techniques. Therefore, they offer a clear route to realizing high-quality, practically monochromatic organic single-photon light sources.

papers.title: Chance-Constrained Stochastic MPC to Deterministic Second-Order Cone Programming Equivalents for Lossy Satellite Links
papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle navigation under lossy satellite backhauls demands robust probabilistic safety guarantees. This paper introduces a rigorous chance-constrained Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework that reformulates stochastic collision avoidance into deterministic Second-Order Cone Programming (SOCP) equivalents. By integrating satellite-terrestrial telemetry via NigComSat-1R parameters, the proposed architecture guarantees recursive feasibility and robust collision avoidance within 4D Cylindrical Volume Exclusion (CVE) models under packet jitter, Age-of-Information (AoI) degradation, and telemetry latency. Comprehensive MATLAB numerical simulations validate that the derived SOCP formulation maintains strict spatial safety margins under severe packet dropout rates while satisfying real-time onboard solver execution limits. Ultimately, this approach provides a reliable paradigm shift for sub-national Unmanned Traffic Management (UTM) airspace integration.

papers.title: Writing expectations in ESL classrooms: a comparative analysis of students and lecturers' perspectives in colleges of education in Ghana
papers.abstract: Second language writing has gained much importance in a communicative world yet it poses difficulty to most students because of its complex-thinking nature. This mixed methods study examines the writing expectations of ESL lecturers and students in Colleges of Education (CoE) classrooms in Ghana. Using purposive and stratified random sampling for qualitative and quantitative data, respectively, a total of one-hundred and fifty-five (155) participants comprising 138 students and 17 lecturers constituted the sample size in this study. Quantitative data covering six thematic areas were analyzed using SPSS to determine frequencies, means and standard deviations. The findings reveal that students place greater importance on feedback in writing compared to their lecturers. Student-teachers also expect their English lecturers to provide models of effective writing. Significant differences in writing expectations were noted, primarily favouring students, in six thematic areas: feedback, learner practice, teacher modeling, grammar, mechanics and revising and editing. However, lecturers placed greater emphasis on organization, unity and coherence in writing. Both groups agreed on the critical importance of editing, proofreading, logical grouping, and clear introductions and conclusions. The study highlights the need for ESL lecturers to hold regular writing workshops, engage students in one-on-one writing sessions, provide deliberate feedback, and implement collaborative and active learning strategies. These recommendations aim to bridge the gap in writing expectations among students in Colleges of Education.

papers.title: A systematic framework for constructing reactive machine learning interatomic potentials
papers.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have emerged as an essential tool for extending the reach of atomistic simulations, offering near quantum level accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. However, constructing reactive and transferable MLIPs that describe rare events, transition states, and high energy intermediates remains a significant challenge. While the active learning (AL) protocol has proven effective for iterative MLIP refinement, its integration with enhanced sampling techniques has typically been implemented in an ad hoc and problem specific manner, which limits its reproducibility and generalizability. Here, we present a systematic methodology for automated construction of reactive MLIPs using SPARC, an open-source workflow package that integrates AL with enhanced sampling through the PLUMED library. SPARC combines (i) query-by-committee uncertainty estimations to identify configurations where the ensemble of ML models disagrees, with (ii) enhanced sampling methods to access reactive regions of the potential energy surface that are otherwise inaccessible in unbiased molecular dynamics. We demonstrate the robustness of the workflow across three chemically distinct reactive systems, showing that stable and accurate reactive MLIPs can be constructed from minimal initial training data. In all cases, the workflow discovers high-energy configurations, including transition states.
